results.title: Confirmatory Factor Analytic Procedures for the Determination of Measurement Invariance | Request PDF
results.content: For the scale's measurement invariance, a Multi-Group Confirmatory Factor Analysis (MG-CFA) was performed using R Studio to evaluate whether the Financial Literacy model, previously confirmed through CFA, exhibited measurement invariance across genders. Chinese college students (N = 1039) completed the mainland Chinese version of the MOPDS for item analysis, reliability and validity tests, and measurement invariance analysis, and after a one-month interval, around 10% of the sample (n = 110) were invited to retest. The statistical analysis includes: Kolmogorov–Smirnov normality test, the missing rates and descriptive statistics of the study variables, confirmatory factor analysis, the gender measurement invariance, longitudinal measurement invariance, and correlation of each factor within the PCL-5. Moreover, we confirmed the scale’s high criterion-related validity linking greater anti-vaccination scores to previous vaccination behaviors, and we confirmed measurement invariance by running a multi-group confirmatory factor analysis comparing our current data with existing data. Results: For each version, we produced version-specific psychometric reports which include the following: (1) descriptive item and demographics analyses, (2) factor structure evidence using confirmatory factor analyses, (3) measurement invariance testing across languages using multiple-group confirmatory factor analyses and alignment optimization, and (4) reliability analyses using coefficients α and ω. For measurement invariance, research data were tested with Multiple Group Confirmatory Factor Analysis (MG-CFA), one of the Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) techniques. However, poorer measurement quality, for example, the magnitude of the factor loadings, has been shown to lead to worse data-model fit and, as such, the quality of measurement was also considered when testing invariance across groups (Kang et al. The two most popular methods for testing measurement invariance of cross-cultural data are methods for detecting differential item functioning (DIF) [22], developed in the context of item response theory (IRT) [23], and Multiple-group CFA [24]. Specifically, we demonstrate procedures for (a) using “sensitivity analyses” to establish stable and substantively well-fitting baseline models, (b) determining partially invariant measurement parameters, and (c) testing for the invariance of factor covariance and mean structures, given partial measurement invariance. Measurement invariance is usually tested using Multigroup Confirmatory Factor Analysis, which examines the change in the goodness-of-fit index (GFI) when cross-group constraints are imposed on a measurement model.

results.title: Measurement Invariance: Complete Guide to Cross-Group Test Validity | Cogn-IQ
results.content: # Measurement Invariance. Measurement invariance is the statistical property ensuring that a test measures the same construct across different groups, times, or conditions. Measurement invariance, also known as measurement equivalence, is a fundamental psychometric property that determines whether a test measures the same construct in the same way across different groups, occasions, or conditions. Without establishing measurement invariance, comparing scores between groups may lead to invalid conclusions about group differences. * Learn methods for testing invariance using confirmatory factor analysis. * Apply invariance testing to ensure fair and valid assessments. Configural invariance, the most basic level, establishes that the same factor structure exists across groups. Metric invariance (weak invariance) requires that factor loadings are equivalent across groups. Scalar invariance (strong invariance) requires both equal factor loadings and equal item intercepts across groups. Strict invariance additionally requires equal residual variances across groups, meaning measurement error is consistent. The most common approach to testing measurement invariance involves multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MG-CFA). Testing proceeds hierarchically: first establishing configural invariance, then metric, scalar, and optionally strict invariance. Beyond MG-CFA, other methods include Item Response Theory (IRT) approaches for detecting differential item functioning (DIF), alignment optimization for many groups, and Bayesian approaches that incorporate prior information about invariance. * Invariance across many groups requires specialized methods. Establishing invariance ensures that observed score differences reflect true cultural differences rather than measurement artifacts. Invariance testing is fundamental to ensuring test fairness across demographic groups. Violations of measurement invariance indicate potential test bias, where individuals from different groups with equal ability levels receive different scores. During scale development, establishing measurement invariance across relevant groups strengthens validity evidence. Proper model identification is essential for invariance testing. Multiple fit indices should be evaluated when testing invariance. Effect sizes for non-invariance, such as dMACS for mean differences or R-square changes, provide practical significance beyond statistical tests. Recommended Sample Sizes for Invariance Testing. Recent methodological advances include approximate measurement invariance using Bayesian methods, alignment optimization for many groups, and moderated nonlinear factor analysis for continuous moderators. Measurement invariance testing is essential for ethical test use but requires expertise in psychometric methods.

results.title: Why aren’t MIMIC models used more often? | Statistical Horizons
results.content: For variables like depression that are typically measured by multiple-item scales, the traditional approach to invariance has been to estimate a confirmatory factor model in each group. Here we’ll see how MIMICs can detect bias across groups in how observed indicators measure latent constructs. * Two or more observed indicators of the latent variable (at least three are needed for testing measurement invariance). MIMIC models combine features of confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modeling (SEM) in order to test whether groups of interest have similar latent means and similar responses to observed items (after adjusting for group differences in the latent means) (Gallo, Anthony & Muthén, 1994; Kaplan, 2008). Formally, MIMICs test for scalar invariance, or whether item intercepts are equivalent after adjusting for any latent mean differences (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016). Scalar invariance indicates that groups that have the same (after adjustment) latent mean will have similar responses to the items that measure that latent construct. For example, after you adjust for differences between latent depression for men and women, scalar invariance indicates that men and women should give similar responses to individual items assessing mood. In addition to their simplicity, MIMIC models have lower sample size requirements–you don’t need to divide a sample into multiple groups (as you do in measurement invariance testing) in order to test for measurement equivalence across groups of interest. This step gives us the test of scalar invariance, i.e., whether item intercepts are invariant across the two groups. Testing how well depression is measured by these four indicators corresponds to step one in the MIMIC process. In step three, the path from the covariate to the latent variable is retained, in order to adjust the latent means to be equal when testing for differences in the observed items that measure the latent variable. Thus, MIMIC models could provide evidence for DIF even if metric invariance doesn’t hold. Further, in a full structural equation modeling specification, paths from the covariate to the latent mean and to items exhibiting DIF can be retained, to adjust for and “explain away” intercept bias in items when subsequently estimating regression relations among latent constructs (Gallo et al., 1994).
